html:
Ashoka's pillar at Lumbini is a stone column that the Maurya emperor Ashoka set up at Lumbini, in today's southern Nepal, to mark the birthplace of the Buddha. Its inscription dates to the twentieth year of his reign, about 249 BCE.

The short text, in Brahmi script, says that the king came here in person to worship because "here the Buddha, the sage of the Shakyas, was born". He had a stone railing and the pillar raised, and he exempted the village of Lumbini from tax, reducing its share of the harvest to an eighth.

Over the centuries the site was overgrown and forgotten. In 1896 the pillar was found again, and the inscription settled where Lumbini had been. It is among the strongest early evidence for the Buddha's life as a real person in a real place.

Lumbini is now a major pilgrimage site and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with the Maya Devi temple beside the pillar. It belongs with the other Edicts of Ashoka, which tell of his turn to Buddhism.
